files.lesson.md: --- order: 32 unit: error9 node: AC9M9M04 n2 uses: [AC9M9M04 n1] assumes: [AC9M9M04 n1] connection: part-tolerance title: Absolute and relative error summary: "Absolute error is how far a measurement is from the true value. Relative error divides that by the true value, so it shows how big the error is for the size of the thing." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Is a 1 mm mistake a big deal? On a bolt hole, yes. On a house, no." --- A 1 mm mistake on a bolt hole ruins the part. A 1 mm mistake on a 2 m beam is nothing. The same error means different things for different sizes. Have a guess how to compare them, and we'll come back to it at the end. (The sizes are made up for the task.) ## Predict: which is worse ```step stage: predict insight: "Choosing which 1 mm error is worse shows whether students judge by the size of the error alone or by its size compared with the thing." check: type: predict q: "A 20 mm hole is made 1 mm too big. A 2000 mm beam is cut 1 mm too long. Which error matters more?" options: - "The hole: 1 mm is a much bigger share of 20 mm" - "The beam: it is longer" - "They matter the same: both are 1 mm" - "Neither matters" actual: "The hole. Both errors are 1 mm, but 1 mm is 1/20 of the hole and only 1/2000 of the beam. The relative error is 100 times bigger for the hole." ``` ## Run: find the error ```step stage: run insight: "Absolute error is the difference between the measured and the true value, ignoring the sign." check: { type: number, q: "A hole should be $20$ mm. It is measured as $20.04$ mm. What is the absolute error? (mm)", answer: 0.04, tolerance: 0.001, explain: "|20.04 − 20| = 0.04 mm." } ``` ## Investigate: size matters ```step stage: investigate insight: "Relative error is the absolute error divided by the true value: a small error on a small thing can be a big relative error." tasks: - check: type: number q: "The hole's absolute error is $0.04$ mm and its true size is $20$ mm. What is the relative error? (3 decimal places)" answer: 0.002 tolerance: 0.0005 explain: "0.04 ÷ 20 = 0.002." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $0.04 \\div 20$? (3 decimal places)", answer: 0.002, tolerance: 0.0005, explain: "0.04 ÷ 20 = 0.002." } - check: type: number q: "A $2000$ mm beam is out by $1$ mm. What is the relative error? (4 decimal places)" answer: 0.0005 tolerance: 0.00005 explain: "1 ÷ 2000 = 0.0005." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#una" text: "Una finds the relative error of a hole that is 0.04 mm out. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: relative-error-product explain: "Line 3: relative error divides the absolute error by the true value. Multiplying gives a number that grows when it should shrink." ``` ### Absolute and relative ```worked \text{absolute error} = |\text{measured} - \text{true}| :: How far out, in the same unit. |20.04 - 20| = 0.04 \text{ mm} :: The hole. \text{relative error} = \dfrac{\text{absolute error}}{\text{true value}} :: How big compared with the thing. 0.04 \div 20 = 0.002 :: The hole's relative error. 1 \div 2000 = 0.0005 :: The beam's relative error. ``` ### Divide by the true value ### Find the mistake Read Una's working. Which line multiplies when it should divide? ## Modify: compare ```step stage: modify insight: "Relative errors can be compared when the absolute errors can't." tasks: - hint: ["Divide each error by its own true value.", "Compare 0.002 and 0.0005."] check: { type: question, q: "The hole's relative error is $0.002$ and the beam's is $0.0005$. Which measurement is relatively more accurate?", options: ["The beam: its error is the smaller share", "The hole: it is smaller", "They are equal", "Can't tell"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "The hole's relative error is bigger.", "0.002 is four times 0.0005.", "You can compare relative errors."], explain: "The smaller relative error is the more accurate: the beam's 0.0005." } - hint: ["Absolute error first, then divide.", "|9.8 − 10| = 0.2."] check: { type: number, q: "A mass should be $10$ kg and is measured as $9.8$ kg. What is the relative error?", answer: 0.02, tolerance: 0.001, explain: "0.2 ÷ 10 = 0.02." } - hint: ["Rearrange: absolute error = relative error × true value.", "0.01 × 500."] check: { type: number, q: "A $500$ m track is measured with a relative error of $0.01$. How many metres out could it be?", answer: 5, tolerance: 0.001, explain: "0.01 × 500 = 5 m." } ``` ### Which is more accurate ### A mass ### Going backwards ## Practise: errors ```step stage: practise insight: "Finding absolute and relative error from a measured and a true value." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A length should be 50 cm and is measured as 49 cm. What is the absolute error? (cm)" answer: 1 explain: "|49 − 50| = 1." - check: type: number q: "What is the relative error of that measurement? (2 decimal places)" answer: 0.02 tolerance: 0.001 explain: "1 ÷ 50 = 0.02." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $1 \\div 50$?", answer: 0.02, tolerance: 0.001, explain: "1 ÷ 50 = 0.02." } - check: type: number q: "Review: a reading is 12 cm to the nearest cm. What is the upper bound? (cm)" answer: 12.5 tolerance: 0.001 explain: "12 + 0.5 = 12.5." ``` ### Absolute ### Relative ### Review ## Make: compare the errors ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the hole and the beam: show with numbers that the same absolute error is not the same relative error." tasks: - hint: ["Divide each 1 mm by its own true size.", "1 ÷ 20 and 1 ÷ 2000."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A 20 mm hole and a 2000 mm beam are each out by 1 mm. How many times bigger is the hole's relative error than the beam's? (made up for the task)" steps: - ["hole: $1 \\div 20 = 0.05$", "relative error of the hole"] - ["beam: $1 \\div 2000 = 0.0005$", "relative error of the beam"] - ["$0.05 \\div 0.0005 = 100$", "compare"] answer: "100" answerLabel: "Times bigger" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["0.05", "That's the hole's error. Compare it with the beam's."] - ["1", "The absolute errors are equal, but the relative errors are not."] criteria: - "I divided each error by its own size." - "I compared the two relative errors." - "I explained why they differ." explain: "0.05 ÷ 0.0005 = 100. The hole's relative error is 100 times the beam's." - check: type: question q: "Which should an engineer worry about more?" options: ["The hole: the same absolute error is a much bigger share", "The beam: it's longer", "They are equal", "Neither"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The beam's error is tiny for its size.", "The absolute errors are equal, the relative errors are not.", "A hole 5% out might not fit a bolt."] explain: "A 5% error could stop a bolt fitting; 0.05% on a beam is invisible." ``` ### How many times bigger ### Which to worry about **Also used in** - **Manufacturing and building.** Tolerances are often given as percentages. - **Science.** Reports quote relative or percentage uncertainty. - **Next lesson.** Percentage error. ```teacher summary: Students find absolute and relative error and use relative error to compare (AC9M9M04, node 2). time: 35 timing: Predict and Run 6 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 11 min goals: - I can find the absolute error. - I can find the relative error. - I can say which of two measurements is more accurate. struggle: "Comparing absolute errors across different sizes. Ask: how big is the error compared with the thing?" before: > Students need Every measurement is an estimate. The one idea: the same absolute error matters more on a small thing. Relative error has no unit. The sizes are made up for the task. running: - "Predict: show of hands before the check." - "Paper: the comparison in Make is worked on paper first." stuck: - see: A student multiplies by the true value. ask: Should a bigger thing make the error look bigger or smaller? fix: "Smaller: divide." stretch: Find the relative error of your own measurement of the classroom. support: A printed card with the two formulas. leads: | Continues AC9M9M04 node 2. Where it leads: Percentage error. exit: q: A length should be 100 cm and is 98 cm. What is the relative error? a: 0.02. explain: > Absolute error is how far out. Relative error is the absolute error divided by the true value. Relative error lets you compare things of different sizes. ```
